explanations.answer: Demands to know why David let Abner go
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Joab walks in and asks the king, “What have you done?” Then he asks why David dismissed Abner, since Abner is getting away. I bet David was hoping for a warmer welcome home for Joab's men.

explanations.answer: Thanks David for making peace with Abner
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Joab opens with “What have you done?” and that is not how anybody says thank you. David sent Abner off in peace, and Joab comes back with a question about it instead of a thank-you card.

explanations.answer: Hands David the plunder from the raid
explanations.explanation: The plunder is real. Joab's men did come back with a great plunder (2 Samuel 3:22). But when Joab reaches the king, the text has him talking about Abner, not handing over the haul. Joab asks, “What have you done?”

explanations.answer: Deceive David and track his movements
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Joab says Abner “…came to deceive you and to track your movements and all that you are doing.” That's Joab's charge against Abner. Joab makes the accusation, and then he sends messengers after Abner.

explanations.answer: Make peace and serve David as king
explanations.explanation: That's closer to what Abner himself said. He told David he would gather all Israel to him (2 Samuel 3:21). Joab says the opposite, that Abner came to deceive David and track his movements. Same visit, two very different stories.

explanations.answer: Challenge Joab to a fight in Hebron
explanations.explanation: No challenge shows up in the text, friend. Joab says nothing about a duel. His charge is that Abner came to deceive David and track what he was doing (2 Samuel 3:25). The text tells us Joab and his troops returned from a raid, and Abner was no longer with David in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:22).

Yes, baker. Right after Joab leaves David, he sends messengers after Abner, and the text says, “But David was unaware of it.” The king stayed in the dark while all of this was happening. That's one big thing happening behind a closed door.
Close, but the text says otherwise. Joab sent messengers after Abner as soon as he left David, and the verse adds, “But David was unaware of it.” So the king did not know. Joab did this on his own.

explanations.answer: As if he wants to talk privately
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Joab pulled Abner aside into the gateway “…as if to speak to him privately…” It looked like a quiet word between two men. This is one of the heavy parts of the story, and I think it lands hard.

explanations.answer: As if he has a message from David
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. David didn't even know Joab had sent for Abner (2 Samuel 3:26). What the verse says is that Joab acted “…as if to speak to him privately…” No message from the king is mentioned.

explanations.answer: As if he is taking him to the king
explanations.explanation: Not quite. The text has Joab pull Abner aside into the gateway, “…as if to speak to him privately…” It never has Joab walking Abner to the king. Abner was brought back by messengers, then pulled aside for what looked like a private word.

That's the word, baker. David says, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner.” He says it right when he hears the news. He makes clear whose hands did this, and they weren't his.

Good guess, friend, but it's not David's word. He says he and his kingdom are “…forever guiltless before the LORD…” about Abner's blood. That's the word he picks. Guiltless is what he says about himself and his kingdom.

Not the word David uses, baker. He says he and his kingdom are “…forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner.” The word he picks is guiltless. Indebted never comes out of his mouth.

The text goes the other way, friend. David asks no forgiveness for Joab. He says, “May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father…” That's David's response to what Joab did.

Right, baker. David doesn't ask for forgiveness here. He says, “May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father…” He goes on to name hard things he wants for that house, and I think this one's heavy to read.

That's right, baker. The text says Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel “…in the battle at Gibeon.” So this whole thing traces back to a battle. I think that's the weight behind the verse about Asahel's blood.

The gateway is where Joab pulled Abner aside and stabbed him, so that's a different spot, friend. Asahel's death happened earlier, in the battle at Gibeon. The verse puts the two events in different places.
Close, baker, but that's the place Abner was brought back from. The messengers caught up with him at the well of Sirah (2 Samuel 3:26). Asahel was killed earlier, in the battle at Gibeon.

explanations.answer: Tear their clothes and mourn Abner
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David orders Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” Notice that Joab is included in that order. David puts everyone in mourning for Abner.
Not in the text, friend. David doesn't send anyone out of town. They're in Hebron burying Abner, and the king orders them to mourn before him.

That's not what the text says. David's order goes to Joab and all the people with him: “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” Joab is told to mourn along with everybody else. Nothing about handing him over shows up in the verse.
Yes, baker. The text says, “…King David himself walked behind the funeral bier.” He walked right behind Abner. A king doesn't have to do that, so I think it says something.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “…King David himself walked behind the funeral bier.” That's David, the king, walking behind Abner's bier. So this one is true.
That's right, baker. The text says the king “…wept aloud at Abner’s tomb…” and all the people wept too. No holding it in. The next thing the king does is sing a lament (2 Samuel 3:33).
Not this time, friend. David isn't quiet at the tomb. The king “wept aloud,” and the people wept with him. After that he sings a lament for Abner.
The text doesn't have a speech to the army here, baker. At the tomb the king weeps aloud, and all the people weep. Then he sings a lament for Abner. His words come as a song.
You've got it, baker. The text says, “…all the people wept over him even more.” That comes right after David's lament for Abner. I bet it was a long, heavy day in Hebron.

explanations.answer: Go quietly back to their homes
explanations.explanation: The text goes another way, friend. After David's lament, it says “…all the people wept over him even more.” Going back to their homes isn't what the verse tells us. It's one of the sadder moments in the story.
The text doesn't say that, baker. What it says is that “…all the people wept over him even more.” Joab and Abishai aren't mentioned in that verse. The people stay with their grief for Abner.

explanations.answer: Swears not to eat before sunset
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David takes an oath: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” The people urged him to eat something while it was still day. His answer was an oath.

explanations.answer: Eats with the people to comfort them
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says, friend. The people do urge David to eat something. But David answers with an oath: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” That's his answer, not a meal with them.

explanations.answer: Eats a little to keep his strength
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say a little is fine, baker. He swears, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” That's a firm oath. He says bread or anything else.
The text says the opposite, friend. “All the people took note and were pleased.” In fact, everything the king did pleased them. The people were on board with how he handled it.
Right, baker. The text says, “All the people took note and were pleased.” Everything the king did pleased them. They weren't unhappy with how he handled Abner's death.

That's the word, baker. The text says all the troops and all Israel “…were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner…” Just before that, it says all the people took note and were pleased. That's how the whole crowd came to be convinced.
The text says the opposite, friend. The troops and all Israel were convinced, not doubtful. They were sure the king had no part in the murder of Abner son of Ner.

Good guess, baker, but it's not the word in the text. It says they were “…convinced that the king had no part in the murder…” That's a settled conclusion, not a startled reaction. The verse before it says all the people took note and were pleased.
You got it, baker. David asks his servants, “Do you not realize that a great prince has fallen today in Israel?” That's the word he picks for Abner. He's calling Abner great, even after all of this.
Not the word David uses, friend. He says, “…a great prince has fallen today in Israel?” That's a strong thing to call Abner. It's a title of respect.
That's not the word, baker. Joab's story painted Abner as someone who came to deceive. David calls him “…a great prince…” who “…has fallen today in Israel?” David speaks about Abner with honor.

explanations.answer: Repay the evildoer according to his evil
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. David ends with, “May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” Right before that, he says he's weak this day and the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him. That request is the last thing he says in this passage.

explanations.answer: Spare the sons of Zeruiah from His anger
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way, friend. David doesn't ask the LORD to spare anyone. He asks that the LORD “…repay the evildoer according to his evil!” That's the last thing he says in this passage.

explanations.answer: Grant the king strength against his foes
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, baker, since David does say he is weak this day. But that's not what he asks. His request is, “May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” He doesn't ask for strength in that verse.
